threat_assessment:
At bracket 4 your cover story is the deck's own reputation. Five-colour Dragons reads as battlecruiser: the table budgets its answers for a turn-8 Ur-Dragon and a pile of 6-drops, and your first four turns — ramp, fixing, a modal 3-drop — confirm the story. The goldfish says the story is even true of the commander: mean cast 8.967, 0.0% by turn 6. Nobody watching for The Ur-Dragon is watching the actual clock.

The actual clock is Aggravated Assault. All three of your contained two-card infinites route through that single enchantment (deck-facts: Assault plus Savage Ventmaw, Old Gnawbone, or Cavern-Hoard Dragon), and two of the three are checker-verified. Ventmaw self-funds at +1 mana per cycle (stack 003). Gnawbone banks net +2 Treasures per unblocked cycle and kills the table sequentially — opponents dead on combats 6 and 12 (stack 006). The Cavern-Hoard line is still a candidate that needs a stack scenario; do not present it as fact.

That concentration is also your single point of failure: one Naturalize effect turns off every infinite at once, and the deck has no second extra-combat effect. So sequence Assault like a combo piece, not a value enchantment (strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window). It comes down the turn it wins — Treasures or lands already able to pay {3}{R}{R}, a Ventmaw or Gnawbone connecting that combat — or it stays in hand.

Remember the funding trap deck-facts flags. Haven, Maelstrom, Unclaimed Territory, Rivaz, and an attacking Klauth — five sources — all make spells-only mana, and none of it can ever pay Assault's activation, because an activated ability is not a spell. Treasures are the legal wallet (stack 006), and Atsushi, the Blazing Sky is your walking bank: his death makes three unrestricted Treasures that pay the {3}{R}{R} without apology.

What bracket-4 tables answer first, in order: Aggravated Assault on sight; Miirym, because everyone has felt the Panharmonicon doubling (stack 002); Sneak Attack, because {R} for Drakuseth is a rate nobody forgives (stack 005); then Dragon Tempest once your board is wide (stack 001).

Your protection budget exists for exactly one turn — 66.0% of games it is in hand by turn 6. Deflecting Swat is the flagship: free while you control a commander, and the only card that answers the removal spell aimed at Assault mid-combo. Hold it for that job. Do not spend it saving a Signet's worth of value.

Embrace archenemy status in precisely two spots. One: the turn Assault is live with a connecting dragon. Two: any turn a damage-based sweeper is likely with Wrathful Red Dragon out — stack 004 verified Blasphemous Act into three of your Dragons redirecting 39 at one opponent's face. Be honest with yourself about that second one: it kills a player, not a table, and two triggers is only 26. It is deterrence and a one-player execution, not a win button.

Every other turn, stay small. Deploy in waves, let the Selesnya-shaped boards draw the wrath, and let the table keep aiming at a commander you were never in a hurry to cast.
matchups:
VS SWEEPER CONTROL: Wrath-math discipline (strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math) — with a verified inversion clause in your pocket. Your mean board is thin anyway, 1.5 bodies by turn 6 (goldfish 1.463), so wave deployment costs you little. With Wrathful Red Dragon out, every DAMAGE sweeper is a trap for them: Blasphemous Act into three Dragons is 39 redirected at one face (stack 004, verified). Know the boundary — Wrathful triggers on damage dealt to your Dragons, and destroy-all or exile-all wraths feed it nothing.

Your rebuild is structurally cheap, and that is your edge. Aggravated Assault, Sneak Attack, Temur Ascendancy, and Garruk's Uprising are enchantments the wrath never touches. Atsushi, the Blazing Sky dies forward into three unrestricted Treasures — mana that legally pays Aggravated Assault. Eminence discounts every recast, and Hellkite Courser rents the commander out of the untouchable zone for one hasty, draw-two attack (stack 005's refutation names Courser as the deck's real commander cheat). Hold one of Teferi's Protection / Heroic Intervention / Flawless Maneuver — in hand 66.0% of games by turn 6 — for the board that actually wins, not the board that merely looks nice.

VS STAX/TAX: You are forced into the beatdown seat, and you are built for it. Taxes punish your 5-7 shelf (23 cards), but three things break the math. Eminence discounts accrue from the command zone, where permanent-hate cannot reach. Treasure bursts (Goldspan, Old Gnawbone, Cavern-Hoard) pay taxes in lump sums. And the Assault engines need exactly one clean combat — Ventmaw's loop is self-funding at +1 mana per cycle (stack 003), so a single resolved activation goes over any incremental lock. Aim your sparse removal (Generous Gift, Chaos Warp, Swords) at the piece that stops combats or untaps — a Winter-Orb effect hurts far less than anything taxing activated abilities, because Assault is the whole exit.

VS AGGRO: You are the control seat (strategy:whos-the-beatdown), and the math loves you: roughly 120 combined life stands behind three defenses, and your fliers blank ground boards. Develop on schedule — ramp or fixing is in hand by turn 6 in 71.6% of games. Treat Crux of Fate as the sweeper that spares every Dragon you own, and Blasphemous Act with Wrathful out as a kill on the aggro player, not just a reset (stack 004). Do not race; your engine owns the long game.

VS COMBO: Answer-economy (strategy:threat-assessment.answer-economy). Your suite is Counterspell, Swan Song, Dovin's Veto, Deflecting Swat (free with a commander), Chaos Warp, and Teferi's Protection as the fold-proof out. Spend them at the win attempt, never earlier. You also race credibly: your own two-card lines assemble at low mana, so the mirror-frame is dueling pivot windows, not pure reaction. The pilot's white-less, token-heavy pods (pilot_feedback.md) mean opposing interaction skews toward counters and creature removal, not Silence-effects — plan around stack fights, not taxes on the combo turn.

GRAVEYARD HATE (against you): shrug. Patriarch's Bidding, Rivaz, and Haven recursion are bonuses, not the spine — a Bojuka Bog costs you a spell's worth of value, nothing structural. Your own Bidding is at its best in exactly the pilot's token pods: tokens never hit graveyards as cards, so the symmetry clause returns you a fistful of Dragons and them almost nothing.
how_it_wins:
Unlearn the obvious read first: The Ur-Dragon is not the plan, and that is your edge. The goldfish simulator (seed 42, 10,000 iterations, conservative model — cost reducers not simulated) puts his mean cast on turn 8.967, with a 0.0% cast-by-turn-6 rate and a cast at all by turn 10 in just 13.7% of runs. Nobody budgeting answers for a turn-8 commander is watching your actual clock. Good — keep them watching the wrong one.

The real engine never leaves home. Eminence discounts every other Dragon spell by {1} from the command zone, all game, starting turn zero. Stack that with Dragonspeaker Shaman, Herald's Horn, and Urza's Incubator and a nine-drop curve plays like a six-drop curve. Korlessa, Scale Singer turns the top of your library into a second hand for those discounted Dragons.

The fair half of the kill is critical mass. Dragon Tempest, Scourge of Valkas, and Terror of the Peaks turn each Dragon entering into targeted damage; Garruk's Uprising and Temur Ascendancy turn big bodies into cards; Miirym, Sentinel Wyrm turns every nontoken Dragon into two. Below the threshold you have undersized, expensive bodies — past it, every new Dragon draws, burns, and copies itself. The verified stacks show the payoff math: one Ancient Gold Dragon connection under Dragon Tempest produced fifteen tokens and up to 255 points of divisible damage (stack 001), and a single Lathliss cast under Miirym plus Panharmonicon produced two extra Lathlisses and 64 damage across twelve triggers (stack 002).

The unfair half is three contained two-card infinites, every one routed through Aggravated Assault — that concentration is why the computed bracket floor reads 4. Two are checker-verified: Savage Ventmaw's attack mana pays the activation with {R} left over, a self-funding unbounded-combats loop at +1 mana per cycle (stack 003), and Old Gnawbone alone banks net +2 Treasures per unblocked connection, killing opponents on combats 6 and 12 in the verified game (stack 006). The third pairing, Cavern-Hoard Dragon plus Assault, still needs a stack scenario — treat it as a candidate, not a fact.

Mind the funding trap deck-facts flags. Five of your sources — Haven of the Spirit Dragon, Maelstrom of the Spirit Dragon, Unclaimed Territory, Rivaz of the Claw, and an attacking Klauth — make spells-only mana, and an activated ability is not a spell, so none of it can ever pay Assault's {3}{R}{R}. Treasures are the legal wallet, and Atsushi, the Blazing Sky dies forward into three unrestricted ones. Around the engines sit velocity and insurance: Sneak Attack cheats any Dragon in the 99 into play for {R} with every trigger live (stack 005 — which also settled that it cannot reach the command zone; Hellkite Courser is the real commander cheat, renting The Ur-Dragon out for one hasty attack), and Wrathful Red Dragon turns any damage-based sweeper into a 39-point execution aimed at one opponent (stack 004).

Your seat for the first five turns is control-slash-value, and you should love it. The deck averages 4.9 available mana and 1.5 bodies at turn 6 — it loses every early race, so never enter one. Ramp or fixing is drawn by turn 6 in 71.6% of games, a cost reducer in only 33.2%, and the reducer-plus-ramp “turn-5 Ur-Dragon hand” in just 23.1% — so ramp, fix, deploy in waves, and do not promise yourself an early commander.

Protection is in hand by turn 6 in 66.0% of games; hold it for the one turn that matters. That turn is concrete: Aggravated Assault live with a connecting Gnawbone or Ventmaw, or a Sneak Attack turn with a payoff already down. Take that window once, decisively — every other turn, stay boring and let the table watch a commander you were never in a hurry to cast.

combo_lines.001: Open with the clause everyone misreads: Miirym, Sentinel Wyrm copies a 'nontoken' Dragon, and a token never qualifies. So when Ancient Gold Dragon deals combat damage to a 30-life opponent and the d20 comes up 15, fifteen 1/1 Faerie Dragon tokens enter at once — and Miirym copies none of them; the checker confirmed it. Dragon Tempest carries no such reservation. It sees all fifteen, grants haste, and triggers its damage ability fifteen separate times — and each trigger reads the battlefield at its own resolution, seventeen Dragons, so each deals 17 to an independently chosen target, with priority passing between resolutions. That is up to 255 damage on offer. The holding is plainer: the 30-life opponent dies to the second trigger pointed their way, their 4/4 leaves the game with them, and any trigger still aimed at either fizzles. The resolution below walks every window.
combo_lines.002: The question presented: Lathliss, Dragon Queen resolves under Miirym, Sentinel Wyrm, Panharmonicon, Terror of the Peaks, and Dragon Tempest — what, precisely, happens? Panharmonicon's clause governs the whole cascade: every trigger in the chain is caused by a creature entering, so every one of them triggers an additional time. Miirym therefore triggers twice, you get two nonlegendary 6/6 Lathliss copies, and each copy re-triggers the payoff layer as it enters. The tally from one five-mana cast: two extra Lathlisses and 64 damage in twelve separately targeted instances — 36 from Terror of the Peaks, 28 from Dragon Tempest under optimal trigger ordering. Just as important is why it stops: every 'nontoken' clause excludes the copies' own entries, and that is what keeps the loop finite. The holding for the table: the 32-life opponent dies outright, and 64 cannot kill both opponents — aim it as an execution, not a spray.
combo_lines.003: The combo database alleges; this stack adjudicates. The verdict on the maindeck's flagship infinite: real. The controlling clause is Ventmaw's own — 'Until end of turn, you don't lose this mana as steps and phases end' — so the {R}{R}{R}{G}{G}{G} from the attack trigger survives into the postcombat main phase, pays Aggravated Assault's {3}{R}{R} with {R} to spare, untaps your team, and buys another combat. A self-sustaining, unbounded loop netting one floating mana per cycle. On the verified board Old Gnawbone rides along, minting Treasures every connection, and the 40-life opponent dies on the fourth combat at 11 damage per swing. The bounds of the judgment: Ventmaw must be legally declared each combat — blockers do not stop the mana, since the trigger fires on declaration, before blocks — but removal, a tap-down, or an attack restriction ends the proceedings. One funding rule travels everywhere: the deck's five spells-only mana sources can never pay the activation, because an activated ability is not a spell. This line is why the bracket floor reads 4; bring it to tables that agreed to it.
combo_lines.004: The doctrine on display is last-known information, and it deserves your affection. The scene: your Wrathful Red Dragon, Savage Ventmaw, and Old Gnawbone stand against a token swarm, and you cast your own Blasphemous Act for {R}. All three of your Dragons are dealt 13 and die — and that is precisely the point: each was still dealt 13 damage, so Wrathful triggers three times, each trigger living on the stack independently of its dead source, each having its Dragon deal 13 to any non-Dragon target via last-known information. That is 39 damage thrown from beyond the grave while the sweep clears every board; in the verified game all three triggers aim at the 32-life opponent, who dies at −7. The holding comes with limits you must quote precisely: this kills ONE opponent at 39 or less life, never the table; two triggers is only 26; and destroy-all or exile-all wraths deal no damage and feed Wrathful nothing. Its everyday value is deterrence — with Wrathful out, every damage sweeper anyone casts is a bad deal for them.
combo_lines.005: Two questions, one stack: what does Sneak Attack reach, and what does it not? The affirmed half: activate for {R}, put Drakuseth, Maw of Flames from your hand onto the battlefield with haste, attack, and its trigger deals 4-plus-3-plus-3 before blockers with 7 more in combat damage — 17 damage that all stands after the mandatory end-step sacrifice, because damage is a one-shot effect no sacrifice can undo. One {R} for 17 damage and a spent card is the honest exchange rate, and every enters- and attacks-trigger in the payoff layer fires along the way. The refuted half is the holding worth framing: the claim that Sneak Attack cheats out the commander fails on the plain text — The Ur-Dragon lives in the command zone (CR 903.6), and Sneak Attack reaches only creature cards in your hand. The deck's true commander cheat is Hellkite Courser, whose enters-trigger borrows The Ur-Dragon from the command zone, with haste, for exactly one attack.
combo_lines.006: The verified table-kill, and the stack that settles the funding question with finality. The record is deliberately minimal: Old Gnawbone, Aggravated Assault, five untapped lands, no Ventmaw — can the 7/7 flier fund the whole night alone? It can. Every unblocked connection mints 7 Treasures, the activation consumes 5, and each cycle banks net +2. In the verified game the first opponent (40 life) dies on combat 6 — the fifth Assault activation — and the second (38 life, holding only a groundbound 2/2 that can never block a flier) dies on combat 12, the eleventh. One accounting subtlety worth savouring: you end with exactly 22 Treasures, not 29, because the moment the last opponent's life hits −4, state-based actions end the game before Gnawbone's final trigger ever reaches the stack. The bounds: Gnawbone's survival, opposing flying-or-reach blockers, and the supply of opponents — the condition is at least 5 combat damage to players per combat, which Gnawbone's own power satisfies standalone.

card_roles.The Ur-Dragon: The engine that never needs to be cast: Eminence discounts every other Dragon spell from the command zone all game. When he does arrive (goldfish mean: turn 9, 0.0% by turn 6), his attack trigger — a card per attacking Dragon plus a free permanent from hand — is the payoff mode, and he deserves protection cover that turn because a {2}-taxed recast of nine mana is close to unpayable.
card_roles.Tiamat: The five-card refill: cast from hand, she tutors up to five differently named Dragons. She is the alternate top-end that turns one resolved spell into the rest of the game — and a prime target for the counterspells you should expect.
card_roles.Dragon Tempest: The keystone enchantment of verified stacks 001 and 002: haste for every flier entering, plus X damage per Dragon entering where X is your Dragon count. It converts deployment into removal and reach — land it before the wave, not after.
card_roles.Scourge of Valkas: Dragon Tempest's twin on a body: every Dragon entering (itself included) deals damage equal to your Dragon count. Redundancy in the deck's core damage engine — with both down, every Dragon enters as a two-bolt salvo.
card_roles.Terror of the Peaks: The enters-payoff that scales with power instead of count — each creature you play deals its power to any target, and the 3-life targeting tax protects it. In verified stack 002 it accounted for 36 of the 64 damage from a single Lathliss cast.
card_roles.Miirym, Sentinel Wyrm: Every nontoken Dragon you play arrives twice — the copy is nonlegendary, so even Dragonlords double up. Ward {2} buys her time, and under Panharmonicon (verified stack 002) she triggers twice per Dragon. She is the multiplier the whole payoff layer feeds on.
card_roles.Panharmonicon: Doubles every enters-trigger the engine produces — Miirym, Tempest, Valkas, Terror, Garruk's Uprising, Temur Ascendancy. Stack 002 verified the full cascade: it applies to every trigger caused by a creature entering, turning one Dragon cast into a dozen resolutions.
card_roles.Lathliss, Dragon Queen: Each nontoken Dragon brings a 5/5 token friend, and her {1}{R} pump is a mana sink — though note the spells-only Dragon mana cannot pay for it. In stack 002 one Lathliss cast under the full engine dealt 64 damage.
card_roles.Utvara Hellkite: The attack-side token engine: every attacking Dragon makes a 6/6 flier. Two turns of a modest board snowballs past any answer short of a wrath.
card_roles.Ancient Gold Dragon: The burst enabler of verified stack 001: combat damage to a player rolls a d20 and makes that many 1/1 Faerie Dragons — each one a Dragon entering for Tempest and Valkas. A mid-roll connection is routinely lethal through the payoff layer.
card_roles.Old Gnawbone: Combat-to-mana conversion: Treasures equal to combat damage your creatures deal to players. One connected wave funds the next — and she is half of the deck's verified table-kill: alone with Aggravated Assault she banks net +2 Treasures per cycle and kills sequentially (stack 006), and she extends the Ventmaw loop (stack 003).
card_roles.Goldspan Dragon: Haste, a Treasure on attack or when targeted, and doubled Treasure output. Five mana that immediately starts paying you back — and the doubling clause makes every Gnawbone, Cavern-Hoard, and Atsushi Treasure twice as rich, which is Assault funding.
card_roles.Savage Ventmaw: Six mana on attack that survives through the whole turn — enough to cast a post-combat Dragon every swing, and (stack 003, verified) exactly enough to go infinite with the maindeck's Aggravated Assault at +1 mana per cycle. Note the mana is spendable on anything, unlike the deck's spells-only sources.
card_roles.Klauth, Unrivaled Ancient: Attack-mana that scales with your whole team's power — but it is spells-only mana (deck-facts flags it): it casts your hand, and cannot pay a single activated ability, Aggravated Assault included. With a real board he casts two Dragons per combat.
card_roles.Cavern-Hoard Dragon: Costs {X} less for the greatest number of artifacts an opponent controls — often four or five mana at a Treasure-heavy table — with haste, trample, and Treasures per defender artifact on connection. On paper the third Assault infinite (deck-facts), but that line is unverified and its funding depends on the defender's artifact count; aim it at the artifact player and treat the infinite as a candidate, not a fact.
card_roles.Drakuseth, Maw of Flames: Ten damage split across three targets every attack, before blockers matter — the removal spell that attacks. Verified stack 005's star: Sneak Attack puts him in for {R}, and all 17 damage (trigger plus combat) stands after the end-step sacrifice.
card_roles.Thrakkus the Butcher: Doubles the power of every Dragon you control when he attacks — with three Dragons out that is a lethality check for the table, and Garruk's Uprising's trample makes the math stick.
card_roles.Scourge of the Throne: Dethrone plus an extra combat when it first attacks the life leader — the deck's second extra-combat effect, but a conditional one: it triggers only against the player with the most life, so it cannot replace Aggravated Assault in the verified engines. The second-combat recheck remains an open rules question flagged for a future stack scenario; plan the first combat to be the one that counts.
card_roles.Dragonlord Dromoka: Uncounterable, lifelink, and opponents cannot cast spells during your turn — she makes your pivot turn consequence-free. Sequence her first on the turn you commit the wave; everything after her resolves in peace.
card_roles.Dragonlord Kolaghan: A haste anthem on a 6/5 flier: your whole board attacks the turn it lands. The 10-life graveyard clause is incidental; the haste is the payload — it opens the pivot window all by herself.
card_roles.Hellkite Courser: The deck's real commander cheat, named by stack 005's refutation: his enters-trigger puts The Ur-Dragon onto the battlefield from the command zone with haste for one attack — the draw-and-free-permanent trigger without paying nine, dodging the goldfish math entirely. The Ur-Dragon returns to the command zone at end step with no tax accrued, and Eminence keeps running.
card_roles.Breaching Dragonstorm: Enters-trigger exiles to the first nonland card and casts it free if it costs 8 or less — and any Dragon entering bounces it to your hand to do it again. In this curve, 'a free haymaker per rebuy' is the honest description.
card_roles.Encroaching Dragonstorm: Two basics onto the battlefield, then it bounces home whenever a Dragon enters — repeatable ramp stapled to the deck's core action.
card_roles.Roiling Dragonstorm: Loot two on entry, bounce home when a Dragon enters, recast, repeat. The cheap card-flow engine the payoff layer keeps recycling.
card_roles.Dragonback Assault: A 3-damage board shock on entry, then a 4/4 Dragon token per land drop — a wrath-insurance engine that rebuilds your board off the resource you were spending anyway.
card_roles.Dracogenesis: Eight mana, then every Dragon spell is free. The most telegraphed card in the deck and the most explosive: untapping with it usually empties your hand into the payoff layer in one turn.
card_roles.Temur Ascendancy: Haste for the team plus a card for every power-4+ creature entering — half the pivot trigger and a third of the draw layer in one three-pip enchantment. The colour ask (G/U/R) is real; check your sources.
card_roles.Garruk's Uprising: Trample for everyone and a card per big creature entering — the green half of the on-board draw engine. Notably, the obsolescence index lists it as the modern replacement for Temur Ascendancy's draw mode; this deck simply runs both.
card_roles.Return of the Wildspeaker: Draw equal to your biggest non-Human's power — routinely five to eight cards at instant speed — or a +3/+3 team pump for the lethal push. The modal flexibility is the point: refill after a wrath, or close through blockers.
card_roles.Rishkar's Expertise: Draw equal to your biggest creature's power, then cast a five-or-less spell free. The single biggest refill in the deck; sequence it after your fattest Dragon and before your next wave.
card_roles.Rivaz of the Claw: Two spells-only Dragon mana a turn (deck-facts: it cannot pay abilities, Aggravated Assault included), plus one Dragon creature cast from your graveyard each turn — mana rock and recursion engine in one three-drop with menace.
card_roles.Aggravated Assault: The combo exit and the deck's single point of failure: all three contained two-card infinites route through this one enchantment (deck-facts), and two are checker-verified — self-funding with Savage Ventmaw (stack 003), a sequential table-kill with Old Gnawbone (stack 006). Sequence it like a combo piece, not a value drop: it comes down the turn it wins, with funding already on the table — and remember the five spells-only mana sources can never pay its {3}{R}{R}, because an activated ability is not a spell. Treasures and lands are the legal wallet; Deflecting Swat is its bodyguard.
card_roles.Korlessa, Scale Singer: A two-mana Dragon engine: you always see your top card and may cast Dragon spells from the library's top — virtual card advantage that compounds with the Eminence discount, Path of Ancestry's scry, and Herald's Horn's upkeep peek to rig what's up there. Casting extra Dragons outworks making them slightly cheaper — that is her whole job here.
card_roles.Deflecting Swat: Free while you control a commander — note that Eminence does not switch it on; the commander must be on the battlefield, so expect to pay {2}{R} until The Ur-Dragon (or a Hellkite Courser loan) lands. Retargets any spell OR ability: it is the counterspell for the removal aimed at Aggravated Assault mid-combo, and nothing else in the 99 touches abilities. Hold it for that job.
card_roles.Wrathful Red Dragon: The sweeper inverter, verified in stack 004: any damage dealt to a Dragon you control comes back as that much damage to any non-Dragon target — even when the Dragons die to the same sweep, via last-known information. Your own Blasphemous Act into three Dragons throws 39 at one face and killed the 32-life opponent on the verified board. Quote it honestly: a one-player execution at 39 or less, never a table-kill, and destroy/exile wraths feed it nothing.
card_roles.Sneak Attack: Velocity for {R} a shot: put any Dragon from your hand onto the battlefield with haste, collect every enters- and attacks-trigger, and let the damage stand after the mandatory end-step sacrifice (verified, stack 005). What it cannot do — checker-refuted — is reach The Ur-Dragon in the command zone; Hellkite Courser owns that job. As an enchantment it also shrugs off the wraths that punish the creature half of the deck.
card_roles.Atsushi, the Blazing Sky: A 4/4 flying trampler for four whose death is the point: three Treasures — unrestricted mana that legally pays Aggravated Assault's {3}{R}{R} — or two impulse-drawn cards. The spells-only Dragon mana can never fund the Assault engines; Atsushi dies forward into exactly the wallet stack 006 verified.
card_roles.Dragonspeaker Shaman: Dragon spells cost {2} less — with Eminence, your six-drops cost three. The deepest creature-side discount in the deck and a priority early play; expect it to eat removal, and be glad it drew it away from the payoffs.
card_roles.Herald's Horn: Names Dragons: {1} off every Dragon spell plus a free extra card whenever the top of your library is a Dragon. Discount and card advantage in one rock-shaped package — and its upkeep peek doubles as intelligence for Korlessa's top-of-library casting.
card_roles.Urza's Incubator: The biggest pure discount: Dragon spells cost {2} less, stacking with Eminence for {3} total. The goldfish model treats cost reducers as the deck's real curve fixer — drawn by turn 6 in only 33.2% of games, so when you have one, build around it.
card_roles.Sol Ring: Two colorless mana on turn one; the fastest route to a turn-3 discount creature or turn-4 payoff enchantment.
card_roles.Arcane Signet: Any commander colour for two — in a five-colour deck this is fixing first, acceleration second.
card_roles.Chromatic Lantern: Every land taps for any colour, and in this deck that is aimed at one number: black comes on curve just 26% of the time from lands alone, and the Lantern deletes the problem outright. It also hands Haven of the Spirit Dragon, Maelstrom of the Spirit Dragon, and Unclaimed Territory an unrestricted tap — their own mana is spells-only and cannot pay for Aggravated Assault, while the Lantern's can.
card_roles.Dragon's Hoard: Any-colour rock that banks a gold counter per Dragon entering, cashed for cards. Remember: the spells-only Dragon mana cannot pay its draw activation — use lands and rocks for that.
card_roles.Relic of Legends: Any-colour rock with a second mode: tap an untapped legendary creature for another any-colour mana. Fourteen legendary permanents in this deck make the second line live surprisingly often.
card_roles.Mox Jasper: Zero-mana, any-colour — once you control a Dragon. Dead on turn one, excellent from the mid-game on; play it whenever it comes down, it costs nothing.
card_roles.Farseek: Two-mana ramp that finds any of the four non-Forest shock/battle land types — in this manabase it is a colour-fixing scalpel, not just a land.
card_roles.Nature's Lore: A Forest onto the battlefield untapped — which in this deck includes Breeding Pool, Stomping Ground, Overgrown Tomb, and the triomes' Forest types. Best two-mana ramp spell in the list.
card_roles.Skyshroud Claim: Two Forests onto the battlefield untapped — the four-mana play that jumps you from turn 4 to a turn-5 discounted haymaker. The obsolescence index lists Farseek and Nature's Lore as its modern peers; the deck runs all three because the redundancy is the point.
card_roles.Counterspell: One of four counters guarding a slow deck's pivot: per the strategic frame, hold it for the spell that ends the game, not the value piece.
card_roles.Swan Song: One mana, counters the enchantment, instant, or sorcery that kills the table; the 2/2 Bird is a bargain against a game-ending spell.
card_roles.Dovin's Veto: The uncounterable counter — the one you hold for the counter-war over your Tiamat or their wincon.
card_roles.Swords to Plowshares: The cleanest single-target answer in the game: exile the commander or the combo piece that threatens your long game.
card_roles.Generous Gift: Destroy any permanent — land, enchantment, planeswalker, problem — for three mana; a 3/3 Elephant is nothing to a table full of Dragons.
card_roles.Chaos Warp: The catch-all for what red-green-heavy decks normally can't touch: shuffle away any permanent at instant speed and gamble on the reveal.
card_roles.Blasphemous Act: Thirteen damage to everything, usually for one or two mana at a full table. Your Dragons die too — sequence it before the wave, pair it with an indestructible effect, or best of all cast it with Wrathful Red Dragon out, when your own dying Dragons throw 39 at one opponent's face (verified, stack 004).
card_roles.Crux of Fate: The one-sided mode is why it's here: destroy all non-Dragon creatures and keep your entire board. The other mode answers opposing Dragon decks.
card_roles.Boros Charm: The mode that matters is 'permanents you control gain indestructible' — a one-card answer to the wrath that ruins critical-mass decks. Four damage and double strike are the bonus modes.
card_roles.Teferi's Protection: The gold standard of wrath insurance: life locked, protection from everything, board phased out. The strategic frame's advice: save it for the turn you commit the board — the Assault pivot or the commander's landing.
card_roles.Heroic Intervention: Two mana, hexproof and indestructible for everything — the cheapest full-board answer to both wraths and targeted removal.
card_roles.Flawless Maneuver: Free with your commander out — which, thanks to Eminence being the plan, means 'free the turn it matters most'. Indestructible for the team through the wrath.
card_roles.Eerie Interlude: Blink your board past a sweeper — and every Dragon returning at end step re-triggers the entire enters-payoff layer. Defence that doubles as a second wave.
card_roles.Patriarch's Bidding: The rebuild: every Dragon in your graveyard returns to play at once — and each one re-triggers Tempest, Valkas, Terror, and Miirym. The card that turns an opposing wrath into your best turn. Mind the {B}{B}: black is the deck's thinnest colour on lands.
card_roles.Sarkhan's Triumph: Three mana, any Dragon to hand at instant speed — fetch the engine piece the board is missing: Miirym for mass, Dromoka for safety, Old Gnawbone for the verified table-kill.
card_roles.Worldly Tutor: One mana for any creature on top of your library — and with Korlessa on the battlefield, 'on top' means 'castable'. Usually finds Miirym, Gnawbone, or the Dragon your combat math needs.
card_roles.Enlightened Tutor: One mana for any artifact or enchantment on top: Aggravated Assault above all — the combo exit is an enchantment — or Dragon Tempest, Panharmonicon, Urza's Incubator, Sneak Attack. The cheapest way to assemble the verified engines on schedule.
card_roles.Haven of the Spirit Dragon: Any colour for Dragon creature spells only (deck-facts: this mana can never pay an activated ability, including its own), plus a sacrifice mode that rebuys a dead Dragon from the graveyard.
card_roles.Maelstrom of the Spirit Dragon: Any colour for Dragon or Omen spells only, with a late-game sacrifice that tutors any Dragon to hand. Same restriction warning as Haven: spells only, never abilities.
card_roles.Unclaimed Territory: Any colour for creature spells of the chosen type — name Dragons and it fixes everything you actually cast, though the restricted mana pays for spells only, never Aggravated Assault.
card_roles.Path of Ancestry: Five-colour fixing that scries every time it casts a Dragon — with 22 Dragon-typed maindeck cards, that is most of your spells, and the scry feeds Korlessa's top-of-library casting. Enters tapped; play it on a quiet turn.
card_roles.Command Tower: The best land in the deck: every commander colour, untapped, no questions.
card_roles.The World Tree: Taps for {G} early; at six lands it turns your entire manabase into any-colour sources — the deck's second Chromatic Lantern. (The God-tutor line is flavour text in a deck with no Gods... except Tiamat, technically a Dragon God, but the ten-mana activation is not a plan.)
card_roles.City of Brass: Any colour for 1 damage per tap — pay the life, cast the Dragon; the deck's life total is a resource its 24 threat bodies defend.
card_roles.Forbidden Orchard: Any colour, and the opponent's 1/1 Spirit is close to irrelevant at a table where your average body is a 5/5 flier.
card_roles.Exotic Orchard: Any colour a rival's lands could make — at a four-player table, nearly always the colour you need.
card_roles.Reflecting Pool: Any type your other lands could produce — with The World Tree online, that is everything.
card_roles.Fabled Passage: Fetches a basic, untapped once you hit four lands; also the shuffle that resets a bad Herald's Horn or Korlessa peek.
card_roles.Jetmir's Garden: A Naya triome with cycling — three colours when you need fixing, a fresh card for {3} when you don't.
card_roles.Ziatora's Proving Ground: The Jund triome, cycling included — and it covers black, the deck's thinnest colour on land sources.
card_roles.Savage Lands: Jund fixing on a budget; enters tapped, so lead with it on turns you're not casting.
card_roles.Canopy Vista: Selesnya battle land — untapped from turn 3 on with two basics down.
card_roles.Cinder Glade: Gruul battle land; same rule — count your basics before sequencing.
card_roles.Blood Crypt: Shock land, Rakdos: pay 2 life for untapped black — the colour deck-facts says the lands are shortest on.
card_roles.Breeding Pool: Shock land, Simic — the untapped {G}/{U} that casts a turn-4 Miirym or a turn-2 Korlessa.
card_roles.Overgrown Tomb: Shock land, Golgari — a Forest for Nature's Lore that also fixes black.
card_roles.Steam Vents: Shock land, Izzet — untapped Izzet mana for counterspell turns.
card_roles.Stomping Ground: Shock land, Gruul — a Nature's Lore-fetchable Forest in the deck's two heaviest colours.
card_roles.Clifftop Retreat: Boros check land — untapped alongside any Mountain or Plains type, which this manabase provides in quantity.
card_roles.Glacial Fortress: Azorius check land for the counterspell colours.
card_roles.Rootbound Crag: Gruul check land — nearly always untapped in a 20-red, 18-green source base.
card_roles.Forest: Four basics anchor the battle lands, Fabled Passage, and Farseek's cousins; red and green carry the deck's heaviest pip load (deck-facts: 47 and 22 total pips), so basics skew accordingly.
card_roles.Mountain: See Forest — the red basic serves the deck's 47 red pips, the heaviest colour ask in the list by a wide margin.
card_roles.Island: The blue basic backs 11 blue land sources for the counterspell suite, Miirym, and Korlessa.
card_roles.Swamp: The lone black basic — black has just 11 land sources against Patriarch's Bidding's double-black ask, so guard it.

mulligan:
Keep hands with two to four lands and at least one piece of acceleration — and treat cost reducers as the acceleration that matters most. The goldfish run is blunt: some ramp or fixing is drawn by turn 6 in 71.6% of games, but a cost reducer in only 33.2%. The reducers, not the land drops, are what compress a nine-drop curve into a castable one — land drops decay to 49.7% by turn 6.

A hand with Dragonspeaker Shaman, Urza's Incubator, or Herald's Horn is a keep almost regardless of what else it holds. The simulator's “turn-5 Ur-Dragon hand” — reducer plus ramp — assembles by turn 6 in only 23.1% of games. When you are dealt one, do not ship it hunting for prettier Dragons.

The second thing to want is an early engine piece — Dragon Tempest, Garruk's Uprising, Korlessa, Roiling Dragonstorm — because the payoff layer pays per Dragon and wants to be down before the first one lands. A payoff is drawn by turn 6 in 62.2% of games; help the average.

What you never mulligan for is the commander: Eminence works from the command zone, so a hand that casts him is worth nothing extra. Aggravated Assault in the opener is a hold, not a keep-reason — it wins with a board and funding, not from turn 2, and it is the deck's loudest tell.

Ship hands that are all lands and seven-drops with no bridge, and hands whose colours cannot cast their spells. Five colours is a real tax, black is the thinnest at 11 land sources, and the five spells-only sources (Haven, Maelstrom, Unclaimed Territory, Rivaz, Klauth) only count toward casting spells, never toward abilities — Assault's activation included.

A protection spell (Teferi's Protection, Heroic Intervention, Flawless Maneuver) is a genuine keep-bonus — held protection is what lets you commit the wave later, and it is in hand by turn 6 in 66.0% of games. The simulator's 75.1% keep-7 rate says most sevens are fine. Mulligan for function, not for glamour.
upgrades:
The deck carries no sideboard, so all ten names below are pool scouts — a ranked read of the entire card pool, not a box of spares. The number that shaped the ranking: three contained infinites, one enchantment carrying every one of them. When a single Naturalize effect is worth three combo lines, redundancy is the cheapest insurance on the market — and the construction corpus agrees: a linear deck “needs redundancy that shrugs off three answers” (strategy:critical-mass).

So seven of the ten are second card names for the architecture stacks 003 and 006 already proved — extra combats and Treasure wallets, led by Hellkite Charger and The Reaver Cleaver. The Cleaver-plus-Assault pairing is the most popular line any candidate opens (popularity 34,407), and it puts the verified Treasure engine on a three-mana equipment instead of one specific 7-drop. The remaining three buy consistency where the role budget runs thinnest: draw and early ramp.

Read the evidence tiers before you shop. Every combo line a pick would open is a candidate — “needs a stack scenario,” pick by pick — and no pick moves the computed bracket floor off 4. The ★ reads are judgment, the obsolescence traces are data, and the verified stamps live only on the engines already sleeved. Buy the scenario before you lean a game on the line.
mana_base:
Thirty-four lands, 16 of them entering tapped — 47%, over the one-in-three budget the deck builder allows itself. That tap rate is the toll for five colours on a battlecruiser curve. The goldfish shows where you pay it: mean available mana 3.042 on turn 3, 4.937 on turn 6. This deck rarely misses colours. It misses turns.

The land sources read W10 / U11 / B11 / R20 / G18, and the pip side reads nothing like it. Red is 46.5% of the pip load on 28.6% of the sources — 47 red pips across 32 cards, up to three at once. Green is nearly square: 21.8% of pips on 25.7% of sources.

Source counts alone will mislead you here; pip weight settles it. Green's 18 lands deliver a green pip on curve 84.9% of the time, because green asks one pip at a time. Red's 20 lands deliver 58.0%, because red's effective ask is two. Blue lands 67.0%, white 63.3%.

Black is the genuine hole, and it is worth naming plainly: 11 land sources, 26.1% on curve. Black is only 7.9% of the pip load, but it arrives in lumps — Patriarch's Bidding wants double black on the turn you need it. Six rocks and three dorks lift black to 16 effective sources and 44.6%, red to 27 and 76.4%, green to 24 and 92.7%. The fixing package, not the lands, is doing the colour work.

Two things the audit refuses to count. Haven of the Spirit Dragon, Maelstrom of the Spirit Dragon, Unclaimed Territory, Rivaz of the Claw, and Klauth make restricted mana — spells only, so it cannot activate Aggravated Assault. Treasures from Old Gnawbone, Goldspan Dragon, Atsushi, and Cavern-Hoard Dragon are the opposite: unrestricted income no table can forecast, and stack 006 shows that ledger funding an entire night of combats. The 90% yardstick asks 36 red and 36 black sources in a 34-land deck — a yardstick, not a possibility. Plan around black at 44.6%, and let the Treasures pay for everything else.
